description: The white-bottle bourbon you've seen behind every bar in America. Jim Beam, four years in charred oak, 80 proof, no bells. Vanilla and caramel up front, soft oak underneath, a touch of spice on the back end. Not the bourbon you save for a quiet night with a good book. The one you reach for when you want a reliable Highball, a clean Old Fashioned, or just a pour that doesn't ask anything of you. If you're new to bourbon, it's a fine place to start. If you're not, it's still a good thing to have on the shelf.

The black-label Tennessee whiskey that probably introduced more Americans to whiskey than any other bottle. Jack Daniel's Old No. 7, 80 proof, charcoal-mellowed through ten feet of sugar maple before it ever sees a barrel. That's what separates it from bourbon and gives it the slightly softer, sweeter character it's known for. Caramel, vanilla, toasted oak, and a banana note people argue about. Goes in a Jack & Coke for a reason. Works neat if you want. Some people will tell you it's not serious whiskey. Pour it on a porch in summer and see if you care.

The red-wax bottle. Maker's Mark, a wheated bourbon out of Loretto, Kentucky, which means soft red winter wheat in place of the rye most bourbons use. The result is rounder, sweeter, less spicy. Caramel and vanilla, a touch of fruit, a soft finish that doesn't bite. This is the bourbon a lot of people start with, and a lot of people stay with. Good neat once you've spent a minute with it. Better in cocktails that don't want to be brawls. An Old Fashioned with Maker's is a different drink than one with a rye-mash bourbon, and that's the point.

The bottle a lot of bourbon people will tell you is the best value on the shelf, and they're right. 90 proof, aged for years in oak in century-old warehouses at the Buffalo Trace Distillery in Frankfort, Kentucky. Brown sugar, toffee, vanilla, soft oak, and a finish that hangs around without overstaying. Works in any cocktail you'd put bourbon in, and drinks well neat. The only catch is finding it. It's gotten popular enough that some stores limit you to one bottle.

The high-proof, high-rye bourbon that's been a bartender's secret for decades. Wild Turkey 101: 101 proof, six to eight years in oak, with a mash bill leaning hard on rye for a bourbon. That's where the spice comes from. Vanilla and caramel are still the bones of it, but cinnamon and baking spice ride on top, and the finish has a real warmth to it. Punchy without being harsh. This is the bourbon that makes an Old Fashioned taste like an Old Fashioned. If 80 proof feels too soft to you, this is where to go next.

The frontier-style bottle with the embossed label, easy to spot on a shelf. Bulleit Bourbon, 90 proof, aged at least six years, and built on a high-rye mash bill that gives it more spice and dryness than most bourbons in this price range. Maple, oak, and nutmeg sit on top of the usual bourbon backbone. The finish runs dry rather than sweet, which is part of why it's a bartender favorite for Old Fashioneds and Manhattans. If you've been drinking softer wheated bourbons and want to know what rye-forward tastes like, this is a good place to find out.

The Kentucky Derby's official bourbon, distilled at a Versailles, Kentucky site that dates to 1812 and is on the National Register of Historic Places. Woodford Reserve, 90.4 proof, made in copper pot stills rather than the column stills most bourbons use, which gives it a different character than the big-volume Kentucky brands. Dried fruit, vanilla, cocoa, a touch of cinnamon, and a creamy finish. Drinks well neat, and makes a Manhattan that doesn't apologize for itself. A good pour when you want a bourbon with more going on than the everyday bottles, without spending luxury money to get there.

The full-bodied, 100-proof bourbon created in 1992 by Booker Noe at the Jim Beam distillery in the pre-Prohibition style. Knob Creek spends nine years in charred oak before bottling. Caramel and vanilla up front, with real wood underneath, and a finish that runs long and a little hot. The proof gives it backbone that softer bourbons don't have. Good neat for people who don't mind some heat, better with a single rock to open it up. Works in cocktails too, especially anything where you want the bourbon to be the loudest voice in the glass.

A 90-proof, 10-year Kentucky bourbon from Buffalo Trace Distillery, made on the same low-rye mash bill the distillery uses for several of its better-known bottles. Toffee and cocoa up front, oak running through the whole thing, leather and a little orange peel showing up if you sit with it. A bourbon that gives back as much as you give it. The catch is finding it. Eagle Rare is heavily allocated, and bottles disappear fast at any price. Drinks neat, takes a single rock well, and a touch of water opens it up further.

The Kentucky bourbon that takes a different approach than most. Four Roses runs ten distinct recipes at one distillery, and the Small Batch is a blend of four of them, picked for balance. 90 proof, six to seven years in oak. Caramel and vanilla underneath, ripe red berries on top, a little soft spice on the finish. Approachable without being plain, which is harder than it sounds. Pours well neat, and makes an Old Fashioned that leans more toward fruit than spice. A good choice when you want something interesting but not loud.

A 100-proof Kentucky bourbon from Brown-Forman that's quietly become one of the best deals on the shelf. Old Forester 100 spends four years in oak, full-strength, and is priced like a much cheaper bottle most weeks. Caramel and butterscotch up front, with cherry and baking spice running through it, and a finish that holds onto charred oak. Bartenders reach for this one when they want real character without paying for it. Excellent in an Old Fashioned, holds its proof on the rocks, and drinks neat better than its price suggests. A good bottle to have on hand.

The black-label bottle that punches well above its price tag. Evan Williams, 86 proof, aged at least four years (often longer), and priced like an everyday weeknight bourbon. Caramel and brown sugar on the palate, light vanilla and oak in the background, a touch of spice on the way out. Nothing fancy, nothing pretending to be. This is the bourbon to keep on the shelf for everyday pours, weeknight cocktails, and the moments when you don't want to think too hard about what you're drinking. Does its job and asks no credit for it.

The wheated Kentucky bourbon from Heaven Hill, built on a mash bill that swaps the usual rye for 20% wheat. That's the same move Maker's Mark makes, and it lands Larceny in similar territory: soft and round, with butterscotch, caramel, and honey. 92 proof, priced like an everyday bourbon. The keyhole on the label nods to a federal agent who allegedly stole barrels of fine bourbon back in the day. Drinks easy neat, and makes a gentler Old Fashioned than a rye-mash bourbon would. A Barrel Proof version exists too, three releases a year at cask strength.

A 94-proof Kentucky bourbon from Heaven Hill, blended from barrels aged 8 to 12 years. Elijah Craig runs a traditional mash bill, corn-heavy with a touch of rye, which puts it in classic bourbon territory rather than the softer wheated lane. Vanilla, oak, a little mint and orchard fruit, and a finish with real wood to it. The age range is what you're paying for. Most bourbons at this price pull from younger barrels, and the difference shows. Drinks well neat once you've spent a minute with it, and makes an Old Fashioned strong enough to carry the cocktail.

The 80-proof, high-rye bourbon from Jim Beam's Small Batch Collection, in the tall narrow bottle with the leather strap. The mash bill is similar to Knob Creek's, but where Knob Creek runs 100 proof and full-bodied, Basil Hayden goes the other direction. Light, gentle, easy. Honey, soft pepper, a little tea and mint, and a dry clean finish. Sits at a price most bourbon people consider steep for 80 proof, and that's the argument against it. The argument for it is that some people don't want the heat. A pick for someone who wants rye spice without the fight.

A high-rye whiskey with 95% rye in the mash bill and 5% malted barley, no corn at all, which puts it firmly in the spicy style rather than the softer Kentucky rye tradition. 90 proof, priced like an everyday rye. Black pepper, cinnamon, dried apricot, and a herbal menthol note that tells you you're not drinking bourbon anymore. Bartenders reach for Bulleit Rye for Manhattans and Sazeracs because it's spicy enough to cut through sweet vermouth and absinthe without disappearing. Holds up neat if you want to learn what rye actually tastes like.

A 90-proof Kentucky straight rye from Buffalo Trace Distillery, named for the New Orleans cocktail it was built to make. Sazerac Rye runs a mash bill just over the legal rye minimum, which is why bourbon drinkers often like it more than they expect to. Sweeter and rounder than high-rye styles, with clove, vanilla, anise, orange zest, and a long warm finish hinting at licorice. The Sazerac cocktail is the obvious move, and a properly made one with Peychaud's bitters and absinthe rinse is a different drink than anything else. Also makes a softer Manhattan than a 95% rye would.

A 100-proof Bottled-in-Bond rye from Heaven Hill, aged at least four years and priced like an everyday rye. Bottled-in-Bond means it's the product of one distillery, one distilling season, aged at least four years in a federally bonded warehouse, and bottled at exactly 100 proof. That's a federal guarantee, not a marketing flourish. The mash bill sits just over the legal rye minimum, giving it Pennsylvania-style spice with bourbon-leaning sweetness underneath. Cocoa, cinnamon, nutmeg, dried fruit, and a finish that runs warm and a little maple-sweet. A Manhattan made with Rittenhouse tastes like a Manhattan should.

A 100-proof straight rye, aged at least ten years, made from a 100% rye mash bill rather than the "barely legal" 51% most American ryes are built on. That's where the bold spice-forward character comes from. WhistlePig is based in Shoreham, Vermont, where the whiskey is finished and bottled. Allspice, orange peel, caramel, mint, butterscotch, and oak, with a long finish that earns the price. A premium-priced rye, sipping territory. Drinks neat to show what a decade in oak does to 100% rye.

A 92-proof blend of two straight ryes, one young and one older, from High West out of Park City, Utah. The blend leans hard on rye in both directions, with no corn anywhere, which gives it a brighter and more botanical profile than most American ryes. Mint, clove, cinnamon, ginger, eucalyptus, herbal tea, a little anise on the back end. Some people taste gin in it, which isn't wrong. There's a green herbal quality you don't usually find in whiskey. Makes a Manhattan with character and an Old Fashioned with a different shape than most.

The 94-proof Tennessee whiskey from Jack Daniel's, drawn one barrel at a time from the upper rickhouse floors where temperature swings are biggest and aging happens fastest. Aged longer than the standard Old No. 7, and the extra time shows. Caramel, vanilla, toasted oak, baking spice, and a deeper fruit character with that signature banana note still hanging around. Premium territory price-wise. A step up from the black-label bottle if you've drunk that one a thousand times and want to know what Jack tastes like with more time in oak.

A 90-proof Tennessee whisky from George Dickel, distilled in Cascade Hollow and charcoal-mellowed before barreling, the same process that gives Jack Daniel's its soft sweetness. Dickel does it cold, which the distillery argues makes the filtering work better. The result is rich and oak-forward with vanilla, maple, a little cherry-fruit sweetness, and a small zip of spice on the finish. Lives quietly in the shadow of its more famous Tennessee neighbor and tends to sit at a lower price for what's in the bottle. An everyday pour. Makes an honest Highball.

The red-bottle blended Scotch from Johnnie Walker, built for mixing rather than sipping. 80 proof, blended from up to 35 different whiskies including some peated malt for the smoky character. Fresh apple, citrus, cinnamon, black pepper, and a smoke note running through it. Aggressive enough that some Scotch drinkers won't touch it neat, which is fine because that's not what it's for. Johnnie Walker Red is the bottle that goes in a Highball with soda or ginger ale, the bottle behind the bar at a wedding, the bottle a Scotch-and-soda actually means when someone orders one without specifying.

The 12-year blended Scotch from Johnnie Walker, built from a mix of single malt and grain whiskies aged at least a dozen years. 80 proof. The extra time in oak shows up as smoke softened into something woven through the rest of the whisky rather than punching through it. Vanilla, orange peel, dark berries, oak, and a peat note that lingers without dominating. Mid-shelf territory, more than the Red but short of the rare-bottle range. Johnnie Walker Black makes a Highball with real character. The bottle a lot of people graduate to when Red starts feeling thin.

The 15-year blended malt from Johnnie Walker, made entirely from single malts with no grain whisky in the mix. That's what "blended malt" means, a different category than the Red and Black Label bottles. Component malts come from across Scotland: Talisker on Skye for maritime smoke, Cragganmore for malty depth, Linkwood for orchard fruit, Caol Ila on Islay for peat. 86 proof. Cut grass, fresh fruit, wood smoke, pepper, vanilla, and sandalwood. Earthier and more layered than the grain-blend Walker bottles. Premium territory price-wise. Drinks neat to taste what 15 years and four real distilleries do together.

The 12-year blended Scotch from Speyside, anchored by Strathisla single malt and built on a softer, sweeter house style than the smokier blends. 80 proof. Honeyed apples, vanilla, hazelnut, butterscotch, and a creamy texture that gives Chivas its reputation as an easy-drinking Scotch. No real peat or smoke to speak of, which is the point. This is the bottle for someone who tried a smoky Scotch and decided it wasn't for them, or who wants Scotch that drinks more like bourbon than like a campfire. Chivas 12 makes a soft Rob Roy.

The 18-year blended Scotch from Chivas, blended from over 20 single malts and matured at least 18 years before bottling. 80 proof. The extra oak time over the 12 shows up everywhere: dark chocolate, buttery toffee, dried fruit, vanilla, and a long warm finish that mellows out instead of fading. The texture is the thing people notice first, velvety in a way younger blends aren't. Still no real peat to speak of, which keeps Chivas Regal 18 in the soft-and-rich Scotch lane rather than the smoky one. A real sipping bottle. Drinks neat, and doesn't belong anywhere near a Highball.

The white-label blended Scotch from Dewar's, first blended in 1899 and built from a mix of malt and grain whiskies. 80 proof, light-to-medium bodied, with honey, pear, soft vanilla, and a faint whisper of smoke that's more suggestion than statement. Dewar's double-ages the blend, marrying the components in oak after the initial blend rather than just bottling the mix straight. A softer, lighter Scotch than most blends in its price range. Goes in a Highball when you want Scotch but don't want a project.

The blended Scotch from Ballantine's, a top seller across Europe for decades and built to mix rather than sit in a glass. 80 proof, blended from over 40 malt and grain whiskies. Aged at least three years, which is the legal minimum for Scotch and not a selling point. Soft, slightly sweet, with red apple, milk chocolate, vanilla, and a touch of light spice. Goes in a Highball, holds up in a Whisky Coke. Ballantine's at an honest price.

The yellow-label blended Scotch from Justerini & Brooks, a Speyside-anchored blend of malt and grain whiskies that rose to prominence in the Rat Pack years and never really left. 80 proof. Light-bodied, fresh, and dry, with green apple, pear, vanilla, soft floral notes, and a faint trace of smoke. The dry finish is the J&B signature and what separates it from sweeter mixers. Goes long with ginger ale or tonic, and works where a richer Scotch would dominate the drink. If you've been making Scotch cocktails with something heavier and they keep tasting muddled, J&B is worth a try.

The blended Scotch from Famous Grouse, Scotland's top-selling whisky on its home turf and a name you'll see behind plenty of bars. 80 proof. The Famous Grouse blend pulls from a range of malt and grain whiskies. Honey, toffee, vanilla, citrus, soft spice, and a small whisper of smoke. Smoother and rounder than Johnnie Walker Red, with less aggressive smoke, which is the closest comparison most American drinkers will reach for. An easy answer when you want Scotch without the project of choosing one.

The yellow-label blended Scotch from Cutty Sark, named for the 19th-century clipper ship that ran tea from China to Britain at speeds no other vessel of its era could match. Created in 1923 and built deliberately as a light, mixable blend rather than a sipping whisky. 80 proof. Pale in the glass, soft on the palate, with citrus, honey, vanilla, soft cereal notes, and a whisper of smoke. The lightness is the design. Goes long with soda, takes a Highball cleanly. A reliable mixer with a real story behind the label.

The 12-year Speyside single malt from Glenfiddich, the most-awarded single malt Scotch since 2000 and the bottle that has introduced more people to single malt than any other. 80 proof, aged at least 12 years in a mix of ex-bourbon American oak and Spanish Oloroso sherry casks. That dual maturation gives Glenfiddich the pear-and-vanilla brightness of bourbon-cask Scotch with a touch of dried fruit from the sherry. Light, fresh, creamy, with pear, malt, butterscotch, and soft oak. Almost no peat. A real gateway single malt: approachable, and honest enough to show what Speyside whisky actually tastes like.

The 12-year Speyside single malt from The Glenlivet, one of the foundational distilleries of legal Scotch whisky and the bottle most often mentioned alongside Glenfiddich. 80 proof, aged at least 12 years in European oak and ex-bourbon American oak casks. The bourbon casks bring vanilla and softness, the European oak adds richness. Pineapple, fresh apple, honey, vanilla, and a creamy finish. Almost no peat. Floral and fruit-forward in a way that distinguishes The Glenlivet from the slightly nuttier Glenfiddich. A Speyside calling card and a fair entry point to single malt. Drinks neat with a splash of water.

The 12-year Double Cask Speyside single malt from The Macallan, aged in both American and European oak, both seasoned with sherry from Jerez before holding the whisky. That double exposure to sherry-seasoned wood is the whole point. Most sherry-cask Scotches use one type of oak. Macallan uses two and lets them play off each other. 86 proof. Honey, candied orange, butterscotch, dried apple, vanilla, and a warm dry finish. Sweeter and more dessert-leaning than the heavier Macallan Sherry Oak bottles. A real sipping single malt. Drinks neat or with a splash of water.

The 12-year DoubleWood Speyside single malt from The Balvenie, aged in American bourbon casks for twelve years and finished for nine months in European sherry casks. The bourbon casks build the foundation. The sherry finish layers richness on top. 86 proof. Honey, vanilla, cinnamon spice, dried fruit, and a soft sherry sweetness running through everything. Lighter and more approachable than the heavier sherry-bomb Speysides, with more depth than the bourbon-cask-only single malts at this price. The Balvenie sits at the upper edge of gateway-priced single malt territory. Drinks neat or with a small splash of water.

The 12-year Double Cask Matured Speyside single malt from Aberlour, the bottle that quietly answers "what's a sherried Speyside that doesn't cost what Macallan does." 80 proof, matured in both ex-bourbon American oak and ex-sherry European oak, with the sherry casks doing more of the talking than in some other dual-cask Speysides. Red apple, ripe pear, dried fruit, vanilla toffee, ginger, cinnamon, and a long warm finish. Rich sherry character that stays approachable. Aberlour earns its reputation as a value pour, drinking like something pricier. A small splash of water brings the spice forward.

The 12-year single malt from Highland Park, distilled on Orkney, the islands off Scotland's far north coast where the climate and local peat shape a character you won't find anywhere else. 86 proof, matured in first-fill sherry-seasoned European and American oak casks plus refill casks for balance. Heather honey, orange zest, cinnamon, dried fruit, and a gentle smoke running through everything without dominating. The peat is aromatic rather than medicinal, which makes Highland Park 12 the gateway most often recommended to drinkers curious about peat but not ready for Islay. A splash of water opens the smoke.

The 16-year single malt from Lagavulin, distilled on Islay's south coast where some of the most heavily peated whiskies in the world get made. 86 proof. The peat is the point. Smoke, brine, iodine, seaweed, dried fruit, sea salt, caramel, and a long finish that smells like the coast looks. Thick and full-bodied, as far as you can get from soft Speyside without leaving Scotland. Lagavulin 16 has been the Islay benchmark for decades, the bottle handed to anyone who wants to understand peated Scotch. The price has climbed and longtime drinkers grumble, but it's still excellent.

The 10-year single malt from Laphroaig, distilled on Islay's south coast just down the road from Lagavulin and aged a full decade in ex-bourbon American oak. 86 proof. The polarizing one. Heavy smoke, iodine, seaweed, sea salt, and a sweet creamy malt note underneath that some drinkers don't notice for years. Where Lagavulin's smoke feels coastal and elegant, Laphroaig's runs more medicinal and challenging. Bourbon drinkers often hate it on first sip and come back years later. Scotch drinkers either love it immediately or never come back. A few drops of water open up the malt under the peat.

The world's best-selling Irish whiskey, produced at the New Midleton Distillery in County Cork. 80 proof, triple-distilled and aged at least four years in a blend of bourbon and sherry casks. The triple distillation is most of what makes Jameson taste the way it does. Lighter and softer than Scotch, with no peat and a clean character that puts the malt and grain forward. Floral notes, vanilla, oak spice, a touch of nuttiness, and a slightly oily palate. Goes in a Jameson and ginger that built the brand in America, and makes a clean Irish Coffee.

The premium Irish whiskey from Jameson, aged in double-charred bourbon casks and sherry casks rather than the lighter cask program used for the standard bottle. The extra charring is the key. It pulls more vanilla, caramel, and toasted wood out of the oak and gives Jameson Black Barrel a richer, fuller character. 80 proof, still triple-distilled, still no peat. Butterscotch, caramel, toasted wood, baking spice, and a creamy nutty undertone. A real upgrade for someone who's drunk standard Jameson for years. Makes an Old Fashioned with more depth than most Irish whiskeys can pull off.

The blended Irish whiskey from Tullamore D.E.W., the second-best-selling Irish whiskey in the world and the one that often gets compared to Jameson by people choosing between the two. Triple-distilled, blended from pot still, malt, and grain components, and aged in ex-bourbon and sherry casks. 80 proof. Green apple, citrus, dried fruit, vanilla, and a gentle wood spice. Slightly fruitier and a touch lighter than Jameson, which is the real difference for someone trying to pick. Tullamore sits at an everyday price. Goes well in an Irish Coffee when you want something soft and uncomplicated.

The blended Irish whiskey from Bushmills, distilled in County Antrim, where a license to distill in the region was granted by King James I in 1608. 80 proof, triple-distilled, aged in a mix of ex-bourbon and ex-Oloroso sherry casks. Soft vanilla, honey, light orchard fruit, and a clean crisp finish. Lighter and a touch fruitier than Jameson, with the sherry casks showing through more clearly. Bushmills sits at an everyday price. Goes in a Highball or Irish Coffee when you want Irish whiskey with structure underneath the softness.

The flagship bottle from Crown Royal, the best-selling Canadian whisky in the world and the one in the purple velvet bag your dad probably saved for marbles or poker chips. 80 proof, blended from Canadian corn, rye, and barley spirits aged in oak. Soft on the palate, with vanilla, brown sugar, oak, and a touch of toffee. Lighter than American whiskey, less assertive than most Scotch, and built explicitly for mixing rather than sipping. An everyday-priced bottle. Goes in a Crown and Coke and makes a relaxed Manhattan for nights that don't ask for ceremony.

The flagship blended Canadian whisky from Canadian Club, in production since 1858 and a fixture of North American back bars for over a century. 80 proof, blended in Windsor, Ontario, and aged at least three years though most of what's in the bottle has spent longer in oak. Light on the palate, with caramel, soft oak spice, and a touch of vanilla. Less complex than Crown Royal but a bit drier on the finish, which some mixing drinkers prefer. Goes in a CC and ginger and serves as the budget base for an unfussy Manhattan or Old Fashioned.

The blended Japanese whisky from the House of Suntory, built deliberately for the Highball rather than the rocks glass. 86 proof. Light and herbaceous, with green apple, basil, honey, grapefruit, thyme, and a soft peppery finish carrying notes of vanilla oak and ginger. The Toki Highball is the canonical serve: one part Toki, three or four parts soda over ice, with a strip of grapefruit peel. Sits in upper-everyday range, short of premium Japanese sipping whisky.

The premium blended Japanese whisky from Suntory, part of the Hibiki range and the no-age-statement entry point to the line. 86 proof. Honey-like sweetness, candied orange peel, white chocolate, with rose, lychee, and sandalwood on the nose. The finish carries a subtle hint of Mizunara, the Japanese oak that adds an aromatic quality you won't find elsewhere in whisky. Restrained in a way American whiskey rarely is, where every component does work but none pushes forward. Drinks neat with a large ice ball, rewards taking your time.

The Japanese grain whisky from Nikka, distilled mostly from corn in vintage Coffey stills imported from Scotland in 1963. Coffey stills are a continuous distillation design patented in 1830, mostly retired for more efficient modern columns. Nikka kept theirs going, and the whisky comes out richer and creamier than modern grain spirit usually delivers. 90 proof. Tropical fruit, banana, coconut, vanilla, caramel, and a honeyed citrus note. Bourbon-adjacent because of the corn, but with a Japanese restraint and sweetness that sets it apart. Drinks neat, and earns a place in cocktails where sweetness plays against bitter or citrus.

The US*1 Small Batch bourbon from Michter's, a Louisville producer making bourbon in the high-quality, mid-priced lane. 91.4 proof, a specific number that gives the bourbon more weight than entry-level options without crossing into proof-bomb territory. Aged in fire-charred new American oak made from air-dried wood, which the distillery says develops more flavor from the staves. Caramel, vanilla, stone fruit, baking spice, and an earthy oak finish with maple sweetness underneath. Michter's drinks neat, takes a rock cleanly, and makes a serious Old Fashioned.
